clinicalPearls: Defined by a rise in temperature and often rigors during or shortly after transfusion without evidence of haemolysis or another cause
It is one of the commonest reactions to red cells and platelets and is generally benign, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion
Mediated by recipient antibodies against donor leucocytes and by cytokines that accumulate in the stored component, especially platelets
Leucodepletion of cellular components has markedly reduced its incidence
Fever must always prompt consideration of the more dangerous acute haemolytic and bacterial reactions before it is labelled benign
Management is to stop or slow the transfusion, provide supportive care, and treat the fever symptomatically once serious causes are excluded
Recurrent reactions may be reduced by using leucodepleted components and, where relevant, freshly prepared platelets
reference.pathophysiology: Febrile non-haemolytic reactions arise through two overlapping mechanisms. Recipient antibodies directed against donor leucocyte antigens bind transfused white cells and provoke a cytokine response, while pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukins and tumour necrosis factor generated by residual leucocytes accumulate in the component during storage, particularly in platelet units. When infused, these mediators act on the hypothalamic set point to produce fever and rigors. Because leucocytes drive both pathways, pre-storage leucodepletion substantially lowers the frequency of these reactions. The process does not involve red-cell destruction, distinguishing it mechanistically from haemolytic reactions.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial contamination with septic transfusion reaction
Underlying infection or sepsis unrelated to transfusion
Mild allergic transfusion reaction with fever
Fever from the patient's primary illness
additionalInvestigations: Clerical recheck of patient and unit identity to exclude misidentification
Direct antiglobulin test and repeat crossmatch to exclude haemolysis
Haemolysis markers including lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and bilirubin
Inspection and, if indicated, culture of the implicated unit to exclude bacterial contamination
Blood cultures from the patient when a septic reaction is suspected
Full blood count to document any unexpected fall in haemoglobin
redFlags: Temperature rise accompanied by hypotension, loin pain or haemoglobinuria suggesting haemolysis
High fever with rigors and cardiovascular instability pointing to bacterial contamination
Respiratory distress suggesting an alternative serious reaction
Fever that is disproportionate or persists after the transfusion is stopped
reference.prognosis: The reaction is self-limiting and resolves once the transfusion is stopped and the fever settles, with no long-term sequelae, although it can cause discomfort and interrupt needed transfusion support.
pitfalls: Labelling fever as benign before excluding acute haemolytic and bacterial reactions
Restarting the same unit after a febrile reaction without reassessment
Failing to recognise that platelet components are a common source because of stored cytokines
Assuming premedication reliably prevents recurrence rather than addressing leucodepletion
